learningObjective: Estimate effective HBM bandwidth achieved by a strided access pattern compared to the ideal coalesced case and identify the underlying mechanism.
profileData: Kernel A (coalesced 4B stride-1 load, warp of 32 threads): 128 B per transaction, 1 transaction per warp. Kernel B (stride-32 4B load with 128 B sectors): 32 sectors, 32 B each = 1024 B moved per warp.
stem: Two kernels each read 32 × 4 B = 128 useful bytes per warp. Kernel A reads contiguous 4 B elements (stride 1) and issues one 128 B coalesced transaction. Kernel B reads with stride 32 (4 B elements 128 B apart), touching 32 distinct 32 B sectors, so the memory system transfers 32 × 32 B = 1024 B per warp. Assuming HBM bandwidth is the bottleneck, what is the ratio of effective useful-bytes throughput of Kernel B to Kernel A?

options.text: 1/4: coalesced transactions are 128 B while strided transactions are 32 B; the ratio 128/32 = 4 gives the throughput penalty.
1/32: because Kernel B touches 32 sectors, its effective bandwidth is 1/32 of Kernel A's; the number of distinct sectors touched is the direct multiplier.
1: the L2 cache absorbs the extra transactions transparently and delivers the same useful bandwidth for both patterns on A100.
1/8: Kernel B moves 8× the bytes per warp for the same useful payload, so at HBM saturation it delivers 1/8 the useful throughput.

explanation: Effective useful bandwidth = useful bytes / bytes transferred. Kernel A: 128/128 = 1.0. Kernel B: 128/1024 = 0.125. Ratio = 0.125/1.0 = 1/8. The waste factor equals bytes moved divided by useful bytes: 1024/128 = 8. It is not 1/32 because a 32 B sector still carries 32 B (only one of which is used, but the sector itself is the minimum granularity). L2 cannot rescue a first-access pattern that pulls fresh sectors from HBM.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: 128 vs 32 is transaction size, but Kernel B issues 32 transactions and moves 32×32 = 1024 B.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: the number of sectors is not the throughput divisor by itself; each sector still carries 32 B, so waste is bytes_moved / useful_bytes = 8.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: L2 can help on repeated access but cannot reduce first-touch HBM traffic; here each warp fetches fresh sectors.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: the waste factor is 1024 / 128 = 8×, so useful throughput is 1/8 of the coalesced case.

assumptions: Sector size at L2 is 32 B (typical for recent NVIDIA GPUs) and there is no cache line coalescing across the 32 accesses in Kernel B.
HBM is the bottleneck; kernels are wide enough to saturate it if traffic were coalesced.
One-shot access, no reuse from L2.
nonImplications: Does not imply the actual observed slowdown will be exactly 8×; latency hiding, launch overhead, and other kernels may modulate the observed number.
Does not imply Kernel B always wastes 8×; if consecutive warps happen to touch the same sectors, L2 reuse reduces effective waste.

distractorRationales.A: Uses transaction-size ratio without counting number of transactions.
distractorRationales.B: Confuses number of sectors with the throughput divisor.
distractorRationales.C: Overestimates L2's ability to hide bandwidth waste.

sourceRefs.locator: Global memory access patterns; coalesced accesses and sector transactions

performanceClaim.scope: A100, single-warp effective HBM bandwidth for stride-1 vs stride-32 4 B loads
